children: By Sarah Klearman

Gilt Groupe's exit as a venture-backed company was unremarkable. It sold to Hudson's Bay Co., then owner of Saks Fifth Avenue, in 2016 for a fraction of the billion-dollar valuation it had achieved less than five years earlier.

But the sale helped give way to something far more enduring: a network of female alumni who would go on to build companies of their own. A decade after it was acquired by the now-defunct Hudson's Bay, the fingerprints of women entrepreneurs with the name "Gilt" on their résumés are still all over New York's technology sector.

Launched in 2007, Gilt brought Manhattan's sample sales online. No longer did its customers need to wait in line outside a physical storefront for their chance to buy designer clothing. They could instead queue up on Gilt's website in anticipation of the day's flash sale and buy that same merchandise online.

The company did $175 million in revenue in its second year of existence, said co-founder Kevin Ryan. By 2011, Gilt was a unicorn. In its fourth year, it had roughly 1,000 employees-most of them women.
Gilt was acquired by its former rival Rue La La in 2018, and the pair formed parent company Rue Gilt Groupe.
"The spirit of entrepreneurship and innovation that helped define the original Gilt continues to inform how we evolve the brand today," a spokesperson for Rue Gilt Groupe said.
Gilt's startup culture

Gilt was many of its employees' first taste of startup culture, said Alexis Maybank, who co-founded Gilt alongside Ryan and four others, including Alexandra Wilkis Wilson. The company hired furiously for its merchandising and marketing teams, with women often landing these roles even as its engineering team remained largely male.
Rachel Drori, who later founded the meal kit manufacturer Daily Harvest, joined Gilt's travel division, Jetsetter, in 2010. She was struck by Gilt employees' motivation and dedication.
"I think it is just the nature of startup culture and entrepreneurial culture, but it was my first experience. And I think for a lot of people in New York, it was our first taste," she said.
Maybank said she and Wilson used to theorize during Gilt's heyday that there were more women getting venture capital dollars in New York than anywhere else.
There was something to that hunch. Data from PitchBook shows the New York area led the country by deal count for all-female founding teams over the last decade.
Gilt was an incubator of sorts for female founders, Wilson said. Female leaders were also ubiquitous at the company.

"There's a very overused adage that you can't be what you can't see, but I think at Gilt it was not just one example. It was many different examples of different types of female leaders, everywhere you looked," said Shan-Lyn Ma, who co-founded wedding planning platform Zola.

Ryan-a fixture of New York's technology sector who co-founded the document database company MongoDB, online news publication Business Insider, and Zola, alongside Ma and others-knows what it takes to go from one startup to founding another. In Gilt, there were the right ingredients for a primordial soup of entrepreneurship: a hot company capable of attracting the best talent, Ryan said-and then it was sold.
'It's the PayPal Mafia story'

Many of Gilt's female alumni went on to launch companies. Beyond Drori and Ma, there is Esther Hallam, founder of infant formula brand Nara Organics; Sarah Sheehan, co-founder and chief executive of online coaching service Bravely; and Aslaug Magnusdottir, who has co-founded several companies including the e-commerce platform Moda Operandi. Wilson is now co-founder and managing partner of growth equity firm Clerisy, while Maybank has founded several companies since leaving Gilt. The list goes on.

"It's the PayPal Mafia story, right?" said Susan Lyne, Gilt's CEO from 2008-10. The nickname refers to the group of PayPal founders and former employees who went on to start other tech companies, including SpaceX, Palantir Technologies, LinkedIn, YouTube and Yelp.

"Even though Gilt had a much more limited exit than something like PayPal, the success people took out of that was experience as much as it was capital," said Lyne, who served on Gilt's board until 2016.
Gilt's network extended beyond its immediate employees.

While at the company's helm, Wilson and Maybank began informally advising female founders of other young startups. Lyne hosted breakfasts for women working in New York's technology sector, informal gatherings that grew, in a matter of months, from fewer than a dozen people to more than 100 attendees, she said.

"When you have a lot of young women who want to join this industry, want to be part of this tech revolution, you can't spend an hour with each of them independently," Lyne said. "But what you can do is become a convener, and allow them to share stories with each other."

Victor Nee, a professor of economic sociology at Cornell University, said New York City's technology sector has fostered a culture of knowledge sharing that propelled its growth and helped compensate for the absence, at the time, of established sources of computer engineering talent.

Gilt played a role in that culture, said Nee, who is working on a book about the city's knowledge economy. But there were others, including New York Tech Meetup, which convened some 800 people monthly, as well as dedicated groups for women in the industry.
Lyne, who went on to co-found venture-capital firm BBG, said there is still a sense that women building companies on their own are disadvantaged.

The data backs up that sentiment. Startups with all-female founding teams made up just 5.1% of venture capital deal count in the U.S. in the first half of 2026, according to data from PitchBook. Startups with at least one female founder accounted for 13.8% of deal count over the period.
Those numbers haven't changed much over the last decade: all-female founding teams accounted for 4.3% of deal count in 2016, while teams with at least one female founder made up 16.6% that year.
Gilt alumni would invest in each other's companies, Wilson said, and continued to hire and mentor each other after they left the company.
Ma said she hopes that legacy will continue at Zola, which has a primarily female leadership team.
"I would love for anyone who worked here to be inspired to invest in people they worked with, hire each other, and ultimately see that they want to work alongside great female leaders," she said.
